screens.title: Understanding the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
screens.subtitle: Design classes so they have exactly one reason to change.

narration.text: In this lesson we study a foundational design idea: that a class should have only one reason to change. This principle helps you keep code focused and resilient. You will learn how to detect multiple responsibilities inside a single class, why mixing concerns increases bugs, and how to split responsibilities into focused, testable classes. We will walk through practical Java examples that show a class doing too much, then refactor it into specialized classes like generators, savers, and notifiers. Along the way, you'll get clear heuristics for asking "what is one reason this class would be modified?" and practice refactoring small violators such as a report generator and an invoice. Emphasis is placed on cohesion and on grouping behaviors that tend to change together. By the end you will be able to explain SRP, identify common violations, and propose a refactoring plan that preserves behavior but reduces coupling. Consider: which parts of your classes change when a requirement shifts? That question is central to SRP.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: SRP: organize code so each class has a single, well-defined reason to change; group together behavior that changes for the same reason.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will define SRP precisely, identify separate responsibilities in a class, recognize common violations in real code, and explain the benefits of following SRP. First, you will learn the canonical phrasing "a class should have only one reason to change" and what the phrase "reason to change" means when applied to code. Second, you will practice reading a class's methods and mapping them to responsibilities by asking whether changes to one part would affect others. Third, you will analyze sample Java code that mixes generation, persistence, and notification logic to see why a single class is problematic. Finally, you will describe why SRP aids maintainability, testability, reusability, and reduced coupling. narration.text: This second objectives screen focuses on practice and assessment. You will work through a hands-on refactor: move printing logic out of an Invoice class into an InvoicePrinter class and update the main program to use the new printer. This exercise reinforces deciding what belongs to the data-holding class and what belongs to a presentation or notification class. You will also take a mini-quiz to identify SRP violations in short code snippets and explain why a choice violates the principle. Success means you can produce a refactoring plan that preserves behavior but isolates changing concerns. We will judge correctness by whether responsibilities map to separate classes and whether tests can be written for each class independently. Finally, you'll be prompted to explain one common misconception: that SRP is about number of methods rather than reasons to change. Clarifying this makes practical refactoring decisions easier.

screens.title: SRP Defined
screens.subtitle: "A class should have only one reason to change."

narration.text: SRP is compact but powerful. It tells us to organize code so each class has a single reason to change. That reason corresponds to a specific responsibility or job. Importantly, SRP is not about method count or lines of code; a single class may contain many methods as long as they all serve the same reason to change. For example, a data model representing a user can have getters, setters, and validation methods directly related to the user data itself. But if that same class includes persistence logic, UI formatting, or email sending, those are separate reasons that will change for different causes. To apply SRP, name the class for its purpose and then ask: if requirement X changes, will I have to edit this class? If yes and X is unrelated to the class's stated job, you have a violation. A common misconception is to equate SRP with tiny classes; instead aim for high cohesion so that grouped behaviors change together. An analogy helps: consider a kitchen appliance that both cooks and does laundry. You would not package those two responsibilities together because they follow different maintenance cycles and failure modes. SRP encourages similar separation in software to reduce surprise edits and to localize change.

keyIdea.title: SRP in one line
keyIdea.text: Design classes around reasons for change, not around method counts.

content.html:
Core Concept › SRP Defined
Definition
A class should have only one reason to change. Reasons map to responsibilities that change for the same cause.
Why it matters
Localizes change, reduces risk of unrelated side effects, and clarifies intent when reading code.
Common misconception
SRP is not "one method per class." It is about grouping behaviors that change for the same reason.
Key Takeaway

Aim for high cohesion: methods in a class should change together for a single cause.

Illustrative analogy
Imagine a toolbox labeled "plumbing." Including both plumbing and electrical tools makes maintenance harder. Similarly, mixing unrelated code responsibilities increases the chance that a change for one concern breaks another.
Check your understanding
  • Ask: what events would cause a change to this class?
  • Group methods around the same change drivers.
  • If two groups change for different reasons, split them.

screens.title: Unpacking "One Reason to Change"
screens.subtitle: How to discover the distinct reasons inside a class

narration.text: Discovering reasons to change means tracing the different forces that can alter a class. Start by listing external drivers: technology swaps (database, storage), policy changes (validation rules), UI changes (display format), and service swaps (email provider). For each driver, ask whether modifying it would require editing the class. If yes, that driver is a reason to change. Use method verbs as a quick heuristic: verbs like save, load, and persist suggest persistence; render, toHtml, or format suggest presentation; send, notify, or email suggest communication. When one class contains verbs from multiple buckets, it likely mixes responsibilities. A practical five-step process helps: 1) Inventory methods and their verbs. 2) Group verbs into change drivers. 3) Name the responsibility for each group. 4) Verify whether groups change together. 5) Extract separate classes for groups that change independently. For example, an Order class that includes saveToDatabase(), sendConfirmationEmail(), printInvoice(), and calculateTax() covers persistence, notification, presentation, and business logic — four reasons to change. The refactor should keep the order's core data and closely related business rules together while moving persistence and notification into repository and messaging classes. This process reduces coupling and clarifies where to make future edits.

keyIdea.title: Discovery process
keyIdea.text: Inventory verbs, group by change driver, name responsibilities, and extract groups that change independently.

content.html:
Definition › Unpacking "One Reason to Change"
Five-step heuristic
  1. Inventory all public methods and their verbs.
  2. Group verbs by domain: persistence, presentation, validation, notification, calculation.
  3. Name each group with a concise responsibility label.
  4. Check if groups change together or independently.
  5. Extract classes for groups that change independently.
Key Takeaway

Verbs reveal responsibilities. Use them to partition code along real reasons to change.

Example: Order class diagnostics
Order methods: saveToDatabase, sendConfirmationEmail, printInvoice, calculateTax. Grouped: persistence, notification, presentation, business logic. Each group has a distinct change driver, so the class should be split to reduce unrelated edits.
Persistence
Business Logic
Presentation
Notification
After grouping, extract a repository for persistence, a printer for presentation, and a notifier for email. The remaining Order class keeps core attributes and order-specific rules like tax calculation if those rules change together with the order definition.

screens.title: Diagnosing SRP Violations — ReportGenerator Example
screens.subtitle: Before: one class handling generation, saving, and emailing

narration.text: Let's analyze the ReportGenerator example that mixes multiple responsibilities. The original class provides methods to generate reports in different formats, save reports to disk, and email reports to recipients. Those are clearly different concerns. If a new format like H T M L is requested, you would edit the generation logic. If the storage moves to cloud, you edit the saving logic. If the email provider changes, you edit sending logic. Each of those edits will touch the same class, increasing the chance of regressions. A useful first step is to list the distinct responsibilities present: report format generation (PDF/CSV), format-specific implementation, persistence, and notification. Each of these is a separate reason to change. The comparison approach visually contrasts the before-and-after: before, a single monolithic class; after, a set of focused classes: PdfReportGenerator, CsvReportGenerator, ReportSaver, and ReportEmailer. This split keeps generation logic independent of how reports are stored or sent. That allows changing one concern without affecting the others and makes each class smaller and easier to test in isolation. Consider a concrete change: switching the email provider to a webhook-based system. With SRP, only ReportEmailer needs updating.

keyIdea.title: Monolith vs split
keyIdea.text: A monolithic ReportGenerator has many reasons to change; splitting isolates each reason so changes are localized.

content.html:
Comparison › ReportGenerator: Before vs After
Before — ReportGenerator
public class ReportGenerator {
    public void generateReport(String data, String format) {
        if ("PDF".equals(format)) {
            generatePdfReport(data);
        } else if ("CSV".equals(format)) {
            generateCsvReport(data);
        } else {
            System.out.println("Unsupported report format.");
        }
    }

    private void generatePdfReport(String data) {
        // Complex PDF generation logic
    }

    private void generateCsvReport(String data) {
        // Complex CSV generation logic
    }

    public void saveReport(String reportContent, String filePath) {
        // File I/O logic
    }

    public void emailReport(String reportContent, String recipient) {
        // Email sending logic
    }
}
Problems: multiple format implementations, persistence, and notification all in one class — five reasons to change.
After — Focused classes
PdfReportGenerator — responsibility: PDF creation
CsvReportGenerator — responsibility: CSV creation
ReportSaver — responsibility: persistence
ReportEmailer — responsibility: sending reports
Each class has one reason to change. Tests focus on the single behavior and mock collaborators instead of complex setups.

screens.title: ReportGenerator — Before & After Code Walkthrough

narration.text: We will walk through the before-and-after code to make the refactor concrete. The original ReportGenerator keeps many format-specific and input and output details inside private helpers and public methods. That mixes concerns and makes unit testing difficult. In the after view, we separate responsibilities into four classes. PdfReportGenerator and CsvReportGenerator each implement a single method to produce formatted content. ReportSaver takes content and a destination and handles persistence. ReportEmailer takes content and a recipient and handles sending. The new Main orchestrates these collaborators: the code that chooses a format depends on a high-level policy, not the implementation details. This structure allows you to swap a PDF library inside PdfReportGenerator or change storage from local disk to cloud inside ReportSaver without touching other classes. Tests become smaller and focus on single behaviors: verify PDF output structure, verify saving called with correct path, verify email invoked with right recipient. A common misconception is that splitting creates too many small classes; in practice small, well-named classes reduce cognitive load because each class expresses a single responsibility.   public String generate(String data) {

public class ReportSaver {

Orchestration example

saver.save(report, "/reports/r1.pdf");

Note how the orchestration composes behaviors without embedding details from any single concern. Each class can evolve independently as long as its public contract remains stable.

screens.title: After: Component Roles and Dependencies
screens.subtitle: How responsibilities map to components and their interactions

narration.text: After refactoring, components have clearer roles and simpler dependencies. PdfReportGenerator and CsvReportGenerator own format-specific logic and depend on no higher-level services. ReportSaver depends only on storage configuration. ReportEmailer depends only on an email delivery mechanism. The orchestration logic sits at a higher level and composes these services. This reduces coupling: a change inside PdfReportGenerator does not require changes to ReportSaver or ReportEmailer. To design this architecture, draw responsibility boundaries around change drivers and create a thin interface for each role. For example, a ReportGenerator interface with a generate method can be implemented by multiple format generators. A ReportPersistence interface abstracts saving so it can be implemented by local or cloud storage. The orchestrator accepts these interfaces and orchestrates work without knowing implementation details. This enables dependency injection and easier mocking in tests. A common pitfall is leaking internal details across interfaces — keep interfaces focused on the single behavior they represent. The practical payoff is fewer merge conflicts, faster tests, and safer upgrades to third-party libraries. After: Component Roles and Dependencies means map each responsibility to a focused component with a small interface; compose them at a higher level.. In practical terms, how responsibilities map to components and their interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Component mapping
keyIdea.text: Map each responsibility to a focused component with a small interface; compose them at a higher level.

content.html:
Architecture › Component Roles
Role list
  • ReportGenerator (interface): single generate method.
  • PdfReportGenerator / CsvReportGenerator: format implementations.
  • ReportSaver: persistence implementation for storage.
  • ReportEmailer: delivery implementation for notifications.
  • Orchestrator: composes components to run end-to-end tasks.
Interfaces keep dependencies directional and explicit, enabling injection and independent testing of each role.
Dependency guidelines
Keep dependencies narrow and directional.
Expose small interfaces for a single behavior.
Avoid leaking implementation details across boundaries.
Following these guidelines preserves SRP across components and keeps the system flexible to independent change.

screens.title: Why SRP Improves Maintainability and Testability
screens.subtitle: Concrete benefits you can measure

narration.text: Adhering to SRP produces measurable improvements. Maintainability increases because changes are localized: when a persistence policy changes, only the persistence class is edited. This reduces the risk of regressions in unrelated features. Testability improves because each class has a single behavior to verify, resulting in smaller, faster unit tests that don't require complex mocking across concerns. Reusability grows because focused classes like PdfGenerator can be reused across different flows without dragging unrelated methods. Readability improves because a class name and its methods clearly communicate a single purpose. Coupling decreases since classes depend on narrow interfaces rather than concrete, multi-purpose classes. For example, if an application moves from local file saving to cloud storage, only the ReportSaver implementation changes; PdfReportGenerator and ReportEmailer remain untouched. You can measure the effects by counting the number of files touched in a change, the speed of focused unit tests, and the reduction in merge conflicts. These practical metrics help teams decide when to apply SRP during refactoring and when the cost of extra classes is justified by long-term reductions in maintenance effort. Why SRP Improves Maintainability and Testability means srp reduces the blast radius of changes and makes unit tests smaller and more focused.. In practical terms, concrete benefits you can measure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical payoff
keyIdea.text: SRP reduces the blast radius of changes and makes unit tests smaller and more focused.

Benefits › Maintainability & Testability
Measured improvements
  • Smaller change sets and fewer edited files per change.
  • Faster unit tests focused on single behaviors.
  • Easier mock setups for collaborators.
Teams often track touched file counts and test runtime as proxies for SRP success during refactoring sprints.
Concrete example
When switching email providers, only the ReportEmailer is modified. Tests for PDF output remain unchanged and continue to run quickly, allowing safe iterations without broad regression risk.
Why this matters: faster safe changes and clearer ownership make teams more productive.

screens.title: Common SRP Violations and Misconceptions
screens.subtitle: Feature creep, narrow interpretations, and false simplicity

narration.text: Teams commonly commit a few repeating mistakes when applying SRP. One is feature creep: adding convenient methods to a class because it is handy, which accumulates unrelated responsibilities over time. Another is a narrow interpretation: treating SRP as "one method per class," which leads to fragmented and confusing APIs. A third mistake is combining concerns because they appear related in the short term, such as putting validation and persistence together because both touch the same data; these concerns often evolve independently and should be separated. To avoid these pitfalls, use the "reason to change" litmus test rather than counting methods. Ask: will a change to this behavior cause edits to these methods? If yes and the driver is different from the class's primary purpose, extract it. Also be cautious about premature extraction: creating too many tiny classes can add indirection. Aim for balance: group behaviors that change for the same reasons and extract those that have independent change vectors. Finally, monitor code growth: if a class’s responsibilities creep over time, schedule a targeted refactor to restore SRP before the code becomes brittle.

keyIdea.title: Watchouts
keyIdea.text: Avoid adding unrelated features for convenience; prefer grouping by reason to change, not by method count.

content.html:
Common Mistakes › Violations & Misconceptions
Frequent violations
  • Feature creep: adding convenience features that mix concerns.
  • Mixing persistence, UI, and business rules inside one class.
  • Keeping emailing or logging logic inside core classes.
Misconceptions
SRP is not about making every class tiny. It is about grouping behavior that changes together and splitting when change vectors differ. Balance clarity against excessive indirection.
If you find many unrelated methods in a class, treat it as a technical debt item and plan an incremental refactor to separate concerns.

screens.title: Step-by-Step Refactoring Strategy
screens.subtitle: Safe steps to extract responsibilities without changing behavior

narration.text: Refactoring a class that violates SRP requires careful steps to preserve behavior. Start by writing tests that cover current behavior so you can confirm no external changes occur. Next, identify a small responsibility to extract — pick the one with the clearest interface, such as persistence or email sending. Create a new class with the intended A P I and keep its implementation identical for now. Replace the original implementation with a delegate call to the new class inside the existing class. Run tests and iterate until green. Once the delegate is stable, remove the old implementation and make the new class the canonical owner. Repeat for other responsibilities. Use dependency injection to allow swapping implementations later. For larger codebases, perform the refactor iteratively across commits, each focused on a single extracted responsibility. Keep commits small and descriptive. A common pitfall is attempting multiple extractions in a single change, which makes debugging difficult if tests fail. By extracting one small, well-tested responsibility at a time, you minimize risk and make each step reviewable by peers. Step-by-Step Refactoring Strategy means extract one responsibility at a time, back it with tests, delegate, and then remove the old implementation.. In practical terms, safe steps to extract responsibilities without changing behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor safely
keyIdea.text: Extract one responsibility at a time, back it with tests, delegate, and then remove the old implementation.

content.html:
Refactoring › Step-by-Step
Minimal safe sequence
  1. Cover existing behavior with tests.
  2. Pick one responsibility to extract.
  3. Create the new class and keep old behavior intact.
  4. Delegate from the original to the new class and run tests.
  5. Remove old implementation and iterate.
Practical tips
  • Keep commits small and focused on one extraction.
  • Use dependency injection for flexible swapping.
  • Review each extraction for interface clarity and single responsibility.
Pro tip

When possible, extract responsibilities that have minimal coupling to the rest of the class first — these are the safest wins.

screens.title: Refactor the Invoice: Starter Code and Guidance
screens.subtitle: Move printing logic into InvoicePrinter

narration.text: You have starter code for an Invoice class that calculates totals and also prints the invoice to the console. That printing logic violates SRP because presentation and calculation are different reasons to change. The refactor plan is: create a new InvoicePrinter class, move the printing method there, and let the printer accept an Invoice instance to read items and tax rate. Update the Main class to use InvoicePrinter to print the invoice. Begin by adding tests that verify the invoice total calculation independently of printing. Then add a test that verifies InvoicePrinter outputs the expected lines when passed an invoice; for printing tests, use a captured output stream rather than relying on manual inspection. After moving print logic, remove printing methods from Invoice to ensure the responsibility is removed. The goal is behavior preservation: invoices still print the same lines, but the printing code lives in a dedicated class. This improves testability because you can test calculateTotal without stubbing console output, and separately test the printer's formatting and output behavior. Refactor the Invoice: Starter Code and Guidance means extract printing into an invoiceprinter that accepts an invoice and formats output, leaving calculation in invoice.. In practical terms, move printing logic into invoiceprinter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Invoice refactor goal
keyIdea.text: Extract printing into an InvoicePrinter that accepts an Invoice and formats output, leaving calculation in Invoice.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity › Invoice Refactor Guidance
Starter Invoice (excerpt)
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

class InvoiceItem {
    String name;
    double price;
    int quantity;

    public InvoiceItem(String name, double price, int quantity) {
        this.name = name;
        this.price = price;
        this.quantity = quantity;
    }

    public double getTotal() {
        return price * quantity;
    }
}

public class Invoice {
    private List<InvoiceItem> items;
    private double taxRate;

    public Invoice(double taxRate) {
        this.items = new ArrayList<>();
        this.taxRate = taxRate;
    }

    public void addItem(InvoiceItem item) {
        this.items.add(item);
    }

    public double calculateTotal() {
        double total = 0;
        for (InvoiceItem item : items) {
            total += item.getTotal();
        }
        return total * (1 + taxRate);
    }

    // This method violates SRP for the Invoice class
    public void printInvoice() {
        System.out.println("--- Invoice ---");
        // ... printing logic ...
    }
}
Refactor guidance
Steps: 1) Add tests for calculateTotal. 2) Create InvoicePrinter with a public printInvoice(Invoice invoice) method. 3) Move the printing implementation into InvoicePrinter, reading items and taxRate via getters. 4) Update Main to instantiate InvoicePrinter and call printInvoice(invoice). 5) Remove printInvoice from Invoice and ensure tests remain green.
Key Takeaway

Extract presentation concerns so core data classes remain focused and easy to test.

screens.title: Mini-Quiz & Diagnostic Questions
screens.subtitle: Identify the SRP violation and justify your choice

narration.text: This short assessment checks your ability to spot SRP violations and justify a refactor. Question one asks which method most clearly violates SRP in a Customer class with getCustomerDetails, saveCustomerToDatabase, sendWelcomeEmail, and validateCustomerAddress. The correct answer is sendWelcomeEmail because emailing is a separate communication responsibility. Explain: the Customer class should represent customer data and perhaps validation closely tied to its attributes, while sending emails touches an external system and changes independently. Question two asks whether combining authentication and profile management into a single UserManager is acceptable. The correct response is that they are distinct responsibilities: authentication relates to credentials and session management, while profile management concerns editable profile data; each may change for different reasons, so separating them adheres to SRP. When you answer such diagnostics, include the reason-to-change analysis: state what events would trigger a change and whether those events affect other methods. This habit is the fastest way to determine whether a class needs refactoring. Assessment › Mini-Quiz
Question 1
Customer class methods: getCustomerDetails(), saveCustomerToDatabase(), sendWelcomeEmail(), validateCustomerAddress(). Which most clearly violates SRP?

Question 2

Correct: No. Authentication and profile management are distinct reasons to change — protocols and session handling change independently from profile data and preferences.
Reflective prompt

Pick a class in your codebase and list the change drivers. If you find multiple unrelated drivers, plan a small extraction as a refactor task.

narration.text: Remember these concise concepts as you apply SRP. First, SRP means a class has a single reason to change — group behavior that changes together. Second, reason-to-change analysis uses method verbs and external drivers like persistence, presentation, or communication to detect mixed responsibilities. Third, refactor iteratively: write tests, extract a responsibility, delegate, and then remove the old implementation. Use these practices to improve maintainability, testability, reusability, and readability. When in doubt, describe the change drivers and ask whether they move together. That question alone resolves most SRP decisions. Finally, look for easy early wins: persistence and messaging code are common extract targets that quickly reduce coupling without reshaping business logic. Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts
Single Reason
Each class should change for one defined reason only.
Reason-to-change

Refactor Pattern

Summary

SRP helps you reason about code change. Use it to reduce coupling and make tests and maintenance easier.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to apply SRP

narration.text: Keep three quick reference points in mind while you code. First, always ask the reason-to-change question for any class you touch: enumerate events that would cause edits and group behaviors that change together. Second, prefer focused interfaces and small classes that express one behavior clearly; this enables simple tests and flexible swapping of implementations. Third, refactor incrementally: write tests first, extract one responsibility at a time, delegate, and verify behavior. These reminders make SRP practical and actionable, preventing over- or under-splitting and ensuring teams can evolve systems with confidence. Quick Reference means ask change reasons, expose single-behavior interfaces, and refactor one responsibility at a time.. In practical terms, three compact reminders to apply srp. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chapter 4.2 › Quick Reference
Ask: Why change?
Enumerate events that would cause edits and group behaviors that change together.
Small, focused interfaces
Expose one behavior per interface to reduce coupling and improve testability.
Refactor iteratively
Extract one responsibility at a time with tests and delegation to keep changes safe.
Final takeaway

SRP is a question-driven principle: use change reasons to guide your design and refactoring choices.
